reviews.review: best warhammer game along with dawn of war 1.

This game is probably the closest we've come to having a good Warhammer 40k title in a very long time, which is probably to be expected since this is a Relic title from the good days of Relic, before the "we must appeal to the wider audience!" nonsense made them ruin DoW3. While I don't have too many hours logged here on Steam, I have played this game extensively on console.

+Positives:

-The game without a doubt nails the feel of 40k. You're surrounded by Gothic architecture, people in British accents, explosions, and general carnage and death. The manufactorums blare constant messages to long dead workers, telling them to continue working for the glory of the Emperor and the Machine God. It's everything you would expect a 40k game's atmosphere to be.

-The weapons sound beautiful. Bolters sound like the automatic cannons that they are, chainswords rip and tear gloriously, Space Marines thud and shake the ground as they charge around like the walking tanks they are. 

-Weapons feel right. They feel heavy and impactful. Bolter fire creates showers of blood and gore as .75 cal explosive rounds tear through bodies, each swing from your chainsword rips your enemies apart and absolutely drenches you in blood. Nothing feels like a nerf gun pretending to be a real gun.

-There is no health regen unless you're near death, and even then it's only about a quarter of your health bar. You want to heal? You heal by giving an Ork a chainsaw vasectomy. You want a health pack? Punch a Gretchin until it explodes. It only takes one punch. There's also a Fury mode which you can activate to gain health regen and increased melee damage after you rip and tear enough to please the Emperor.

-You're fairly durable. You're a Space Marine, wearing some of the best armor ever developed. You feel like a tank, but you aren't invincible. You can tear through hordes of smaller Orks without breaking stride, but fights between other Marines or large orks can go badly quickly if you get overconfidant. When you fight traitor marines, or other players in multiplayer, it feels like a clash between titans instead of a fight between mortals.

-The voice acting is on point. Mark Strong is fantastic as Captain Titus, and his squadmates voices were also well chosen. The voices for the enemy NPCs and the few other friendly NPCs are also fairly good.

-The story is decent. It's not going to win any awards, and if you know anything about 40k (or even if you don't) you'll probably be able to guess some of the plot points before they happen. That said, the story doesn't hurt the game and it's still possible to get interested and invested in the characters. You won't leave the game asking any deep, meaningful questions, but you also won't leave the game regreting your purchase. There are plenty of awesome moments, some cool dialogue, everything you'd expect to come out of 40k. The story fits the game. It's good, fairly simple, and pretty enjoyable.

-It controls well. The options menu isn't huge, but the controls are intelligent for the most part. It's not a game that you'll need an extra hand to play, and it works well on both keyboard and controller.


=Neutral:


-The multiplayer is pretty simple. Deathmatch, CTF, etc. The usual game modes. It's not as good as the single player, but it's a servicable time-sink if you want to shoot other players in a 40k game. Some single player mechanics are removed or changed to make them work in a multiplayer setting, but overall it's still decent.

-There is a co-op PVE mode, but it's very hard. It's a round-based game where you have to hold an arena against waves of Orks and eventually Chaos, with the waves going up in difficulty until you reach what is essentially an unbeatable last wave. I've only beaten it once, and we had a hacker playing with us who had unlimited ammo and was invincible. It's a fun mode, but it can get repetitive after a while.


-Negatives:

-The multiplayer is basically dead. The game is so old, and the actual multiplayer content is so basic and small that there aren't a whole lot of people still playing. The game also runs peer to peer instead of on a dedicated server, which can be seen as a blessing or a curse since, while you have to deal with all the problems that come from having the match running off of one of the players internet (so if he's far away or has bad internet you can have terrible ping), it also means that there are no servers to be shut down.

-The multiplayer modes can get boring quickly. There's a few maps, a few modes, and the co-op has even less in the way of options.

-There are hackers. Pretty much explains itself.

-You can't choose which faction you play as. You're randomly assigned to either Chaos or Loyalist when you join a match. While it doesn't effect the gameplay, since the wargear for both factions is stat identical save for flavor like chainaxes instead of power axes and daemon mauls instead of thunder hammers, you can't work towards cosmetics for one faction while playing the other. So if you really want a certain piece of armor for your Loyalist marine, but you keep getting put on the Chaos team, there's nothing you can do about it. You can't even switch teams once you're in the match.

-The campaign is very linear. While it's not entirely a bad thing, it does mean that there's not as much replayability as a more option game.


Overall, the game is good. It has a solid single player, and a decent multiplayer. Though you can easily tell it was made with the single player as top priority, the rest of the game can be enjoyable if you can find a community that still plays this game, or you have friends that do.

Welcome to Warhamer 40k, or as we'll call it w40k, it has six races, each with their own name classes, units, and heroes.  And then we have the.... <pause and slide that to the side.>

This is Warhammer 40k, but it's not.  Instead this is a third person hack and slash, with ranged weapons where you play a Space Marine (or an Ultramarine) and fight through 18 stages.  It is in the 40k universe, but it doesn't require the massive wealth of knowledge or fandom most of these games seem to expect. 

And you know what?  It's the first Warhammer 40k game I really really enjoyed.   Dawn of War is a fine RTS if you really want to play an RTS, or really want to deal with that complexity, however Space Marine brings the user into the universe and creates a reasonable scope of the world for them to enjoy. 

It avoid overly repetitive gameplay, it avoids the massively complex world of 40k which will overwhelm all but the few fans of sci fi with the ability to comprehend it all from a game, and focuses on just a single adventure in that universe. 

And it works!   The gameplay is fantastic, where the main character has a decent amount of options.  You can choose from three weapons, and a number of ranged weapons (carrying up to 4 at a time, with I believe at least 7 different weapons, not counting full upgrades).   The enemies is a little similar, for a majority of the game you will fight the orks (one of the six races)  but there's enough variety in location, ability and configurations that it rarely feels like a slog, surprisingly so. 

Even the graphics hold up well for a 6 year old (last gen) game.   The story is solid.  It's not going to win awards, but it at least has a driving force and while it does dig a bit into the lore (at least i think it does) isn't a distracting trip.  If you like the lore, I'm sure you'll get a lot out of it, but if you don't know the lore at a deep level (like me) you'll really enjoy the story. 

Overall I like the game, I like the game a lot more than quite a few game.  It's definitely trying to be a bit like that "god of war" style that everyone was playing at the time, quite a bit of hack and slash is required, though this game finds a solid balance between third person shooting and melee fighting and it's pretty glorious when you have it right.    I recommend it, and considering it's often on sales, it's a great time to pick this up.
